summary: Updates the registry of Authentication-Results header field properties so one message can report separate results for each of several cryptographic signatures on it. This lets each result be linked to the signature it refers to.

plainLanguage.summary: An email can carry several signature stamps. This lets the mail checker say clearly which stamp passed and which failed.

questions: how to report results for each signature in email
how to tell which dkim signature failed
what is the b tag in dkim
subtitle: A small registry addition that lets a mail checker say which DKIM signature each result belongs to.

tldr.problem: A message can carry several DKIM signatures, even from the same domain, so an Authentication-Results header could show both dkim=pass and dkim=fail with no way to tell which signature each referred to.
tldr.mechanism: The memo registers a new reporting item, header.b, whose value is at least the first eight characters of the signature's b= tag, long enough to be unique among the reported results.
tldr.outcome: Each result can be tied to its own signature. If unequal results still appear for the same signature from the same trusted authserv-id, the evaluating agent SHOULD ignore them all.

today: RFC 6008 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2010. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Ambiguity Problem
sections.content:
The Authentication-Results header field (RFC 5451) reports the outcome of message authentication in a machine-readable form. It did not provide a way to report the results of two cryptographic signatures, such as those from DKIM (RFC 4871), unambiguously.

Because RFC 5451 created IANA registries of reporting properties, the fix is simple: register one more property that ties a result to a specific digital signature.
sections.plainLanguage: If a letter has two stamps and the checker says "one good, one bad" without saying which, you cannot tell which stamp is the bad one.

sections.title: Why Existing Properties Are Not Enough
sections.content:
A message can hold several signatures from the same mechanism. For example, a signer might use two different canonicalization algorithms to see which better survives transit.

Existing ptype.property combinations like header.d or header.i can separate results only if those values differ between signatures. A signer may have good reasons to use the same d= value on several signatures, so a verifier could produce both dkim=pass and dkim=fail with nothing to tell them apart.

The actual signature is an ideal unique identifier, since collisions with SHA1 and SHA256 are uncommon. The whole signature is not needed; the first several bytes should be enough.
sections.plainLanguage: Writing your name on each stamp would not help if both were signed by you. The stamp's own scribble is different every time, so a few letters of it will do.

sections.title: The header.b Item
sections.content:
The memo adds header.b to the IANA "Email Authentication Methods" registry. Its value MUST be at least the first eight characters of the signature (the b= tag of a DKIM-Signature) and MUST be long enough to be unique among the results reported. If the whole signature is shorter than eight characters, all of it MUST be included. Matching against the signature MUST be case-sensitive.

If an evaluating agent still sees unequal results about the same signature from the same trusted authserv-id, it SHOULD ignore all such results.
sections.plainLanguage: You copy the first few letters of each stamp's scribble next to its result. If the checker still gives two different answers for one stamp, you ignore them all.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo argues it fixes a weakness of the original specification, since previously ambiguous results become useful.

An attacker could copy a valid signature onto a message in transit and alter part of it, producing two results for the same header.b value even if the full b= string is used. That could relay an ambiguous result and neutralize the benefit of a pass. A false negative can be generated this way, but a false positive is extremely difficult, so a cautious implementation could discard the false negative.

If a new signing scheme has signatures shorter than eight characters, the entire signature must be used. A scheme prone to collisions would make the value not useful, but the risk comes from the collisions, and the rule to ignore unequal results prevents an ambiguous result being applied.
sections.plainLanguage: A sneaky person might copy a good stamp and smudge it. That can create a false "bad" mark, but it is very hard to fake a "good" one.

sections.title: Example with Two DKIM Signatures
sections.content:
The appendix shows a message signed twice by the same domain, newyork.example.com. One signature used relaxed header canonicalization and one used simple; both used simple body canonicalization. The header reports dkim=pass with header.b=oINEO8hg and dkim=fail with header.b=EToRSuvU.

One of the five header fields covered by the signatures presumably changed. Relaxed canonicalization tolerates whitespace changes in the header and simple does not, so the simple one failed. Without header.b, it would be unclear which signature passed and which failed.
sections.plainLanguage: Two stamps, same sender. One was tough against smudges and survived; the other was not and failed. The short tag says which is which.

data.title: Two results, told apart by header.b
